title: Structural stability, electronic structure, and magnetism of the $d^9$ double infinite-layer La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_5$F under chemical pressure and epitaxial strain
authors: K. Madani, Q. N. Meier, A. Cano
abstract: Nickelate materials exhibit rich electronic properties that can be engineered toward cuprate-like regimes through topotactic and mixed-anion chemistry. Using first-principles calculations, we investigate the newly synthesized double infinite-layer oxyfluoride La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_5$F and its evolution under chemical pressure and epitaxial strain. The calculated phonon spectrum confirms the dynamical stability of the reported double infinite-layer crystal structure. Further, we find a highly two-dimensional cuprate-like Fermi surface dominated by Ni-$d_{x^2-y^2}$ states, with a moderate rare-earth-derived self-doping yielding an effective $\sim d^{1.2}_{x^2-y^2}$ filling. These electronic features remain remarkably robust under both chemical pressure and epitaxial strain. Spin-polarized calculations further reveal an extended manifold of nearly degenerate magnetic configurations with different in-plane and out-of-plane spin arrangements. Compressive strain further enhances this magnetic frustration while leaving the underlying electronic structure largely unchanged. Our results thus identify La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_5$F as a promising cuprate analogue and establish lattice engineering as an effective strategy for fine tuning its electronic and magnetic properties.
summary: This theoretical study examines $	ext{La}_3	ext{Ni}_2	ext{O}_5	ext{F}$ as a tunable cuprate analogue, using first-principles calculations to probe its electronic and magnetic properties. The research demonstrates that the material maintains a robust, two-dimensional Ni-$d_{x^2-y^2}$ Fermi surface even when subjected to chemical pressure or epitaxial strain. Ultimately, it establishes lattice engineering as a powerful tool for controlling correlated electron behavior in nickelates.
main_problem: The study investigates how structural stability, electronic structure, and magnetism of the double infinite-layer oxyfluoride $	ext{La}_3	ext{Ni}_2	ext{O}_5	ext{F}$ are influenced by external tuning parameters like chemical pressure and epitaxial strain.
main_result: The material is identified as a promising cuprate analogue because its electronic structure remains robustly two-dimensional, while lattice engineering allows for continuous fine-tuning of carrier doping and magnetic frustration.
method: First-principles calculations using DFT (PBE functional) are employed to calculate phonon spectra, band structures, Fermi surfaces, and magnetic ground states under varying strain and chemical substitutions.
model_or_system: The system is the double infinite-layer nickelate $	ext{La}_3	ext{Ni}_2	ext{O}_5	ext{F}$, which is modeled as a correlated electron material exhibiting strong electronic correlations in the Ni $d$-orbitals, analogous to high-Tc cuprates.
key_observables: Phonon spectrum (stability), Fermi surface character ($	ext{Ni-}d_{x^2-y^2}$ dominance), self-doping level, and magnetic ground state energy/frustration.
important_parameters: Epitaxial strain ($\epsilon$), chemical pressure (rare-earth substitution $	ext{La} 	o 	ext{Sm}$), and the charge-transfer energy ($\Delta$).
main_assumptions: The calculations rely on DFT approximations, treating the system as a solid-state material where electronic correlations are captured via orbital analysis and magnetic modeling.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the phonon spectrum confirming stability under strain, band structures showing 2D cuprate-like features across substitutions, and energy comparisons detailing competing magnetic ground states.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the structural and electronic baseline of $	ext{La}_3	ext{Ni}_2	ext{O}_5	ext{F}$. It then systematically explores how chemical pressure (substitution) and epitaxial strain modify the robust 2D electronic structure and tune the magnetic frustration landscape.
why_interesting: The ability to use lattice engineering (strain/pressure) to continuously control correlated parameters like doping and magnetic interactions in a solid-state system is highly relevant for understanding emergent quantum phases in strongly correlated materials.

Figure 3 shows the calculated electronic structure of La2SmNi2O5F. Compared with La3Ni2O5F, the Ni- dx2−y2 bands and the O-2p manifold remain essentially unchanged, while the rare-earth-derived bands shift sub- tly downward. Specifically, the self-doping band sinks further below EF around M and A, and the empty rare- earth conduction band moves closer to EF along Γ-Z. Although the absolute position of these states might be sensitive to the 4f treatment of the rare-earth ions, their evolution with chemical pressure is robust, yielding a con- sistent trend across the rare-earth series (Fig. S3).
